claims.text: Premelting and melting in initially solid FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are governed primarily by surface-driven processes.
Selective atomic segregation and surface diffusion are the specific surface processes governing the phase-transition onset and progression.
Suppressing surface diffusion and segregation by capping the nanoparticles will delay the appearance of premelting phenomena.
Suppressing surface diffusion and segregation will shift melting onset to a higher temperature than in bare nanoparticles.
The starting FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are well mixed and compositionally homogeneous.
The starting nanoparticles have a narrow size distribution.
A surface-passivating capping agent can suppress surface atomic diffusion and segregation in these nanoparticles.
Rapid heating rates are representative of high-temperature nanoparticle synthesis.
An inert atmosphere prevents oxidation during the heating experiment.
Bare nanoparticle surfaces have enhanced atomic mobility at elevated temperatures.
Enhanced surface mobility promotes early surface diffusion and selective elemental segregation.
Early surface diffusion and segregation prematurely initiate the phase transition.
Passivation hinders surface diffusion and thereby delays or alters premelting and subsequent bulk melting.
Relative to bare particles, passivated particles will show fewer surface-diffusion events and less incipient segregation during heating.
Relative to bare particles, passivated particles will have a higher observable melting-initiation temperature.
Untreated FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles exhibit surface diffusion and selective segregation before bulk melting.
Metal atoms can diffuse into a carbon support during extreme-temperature nanoparticle processing and strengthen nanoparticle anchoring.
Indistinguishable premelting onset, surface diffusion, segregation, and melting progression between capped and bare particles would falsify the proposed dominance of surface-driven processes.
